startup.name: Aegis
startup.one_liner: AI Agents to win denied health insurance claims.
startup.description: Aegis sells an AI platform to healthcare providers and hospital billing teams that automates insurance denial appeals from intake to resolution, to recover lost revenue. Customers pay for recovered revenue or a software fee. Team of 3 in San Francisco, Spring 2025 batch.

yc_acceptance.basis: Already in the Spring 2025 batch, so this is reported for completeness only. Start from the roughly 1 percent prior for a random applicant in references/yc_acceptance.md, then lift by about 2x for a clear paid pain point (denials cost providers real revenue) and an AI agent wedge that fits current YC interest, and take nothing for traction because none is stated.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because denial appeals and revenue cycle automation was already a crowded AI category by early 2025 (CombineHealth W23, Egress Health W25), and a three person team with no stated healthcare billing background or live customers gives little reason to expect it to win the category.

anchors.source: python3 -I scripts/base_rates.py --years 2022-2024 --industry Healthcare: seed 49% / 53% / 57% (lower / known-only / upper), cond 53% (n=167). Window check from time_to_milestones.csv industry:Healthcare months_to_seed p25 4, p50 8.75, p75 27.
anchors.adjustment_reason: The anchor of 0.53 is the ever reached figure. The window is 19 months from 2025-04-07 to 2026-11-17, which covers roughly 70 percent of healthcare seed raises by timing (p75 is 27 months), giving about 0.37. I keep 0.36 and do not lift for the hot AI revenue cycle sector, per the winners test rule. This probability does not rank Aegis against other companies.

bands.rationale: Small post YC round of $1M to $3M, typical when a two to four person team raises from angels and micro funds soon after demo day. Healthcare seed rounds after 2022 had a median of $3.3M in the Healthcare cohort (n=73), so the middle bands carry the most weight.

Institutional seed of $3M to $6M, near the 2022 and later median of $3.5M in round_benchmarks.csv, which includes the YC deal so it reads low. Healthcare seed rounds after 2022 had a median of $3.3M in the Healthcare cohort (n=73), so the middle bands carry the most weight.
Larger institutional seed of $6M to $12M, where press covered 2026 raises had their median of $6.0M; needs live revenue or a standout founder story.
Upside seed above $12M, seen in 2025 voice, document and agent categories when a lab style team is bid up by several funds.

ladder.why_it_fails: Investors in this wedge want proof that appeals actually get paid back and that the product works across payers and billing systems. Aegis has three people and no stated customers, while CombineHealth (W23) has a 15 person team and still shows no verified funding, which suggests even funded looking RCM players struggle to turn pilots into a priced round. A pivot-then-raise path to a broader RCM product is the upside route.

Central band around the 2022 and later Series A median of $15M with p25 $11M.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series A needs repeatable revenue from health systems that have long procurement cycles, EHR integration work and a denial recovery story that is audited by finance teams. Inside the window Aegis would need to land several hospital contracts within about a year after seed. Analogs such as Arintra (W22) took over three years from batch to its first announced Series A, and CombineHealth has not shown a priced round.

anchors.adjustment_reason: Series B inside a window of 19 months is rare: months_to_series_b has a median of 36 to 47 months from the batch start in time_to_milestones.csv, so almost no company reaches it this fast. Only a breakout would.

bands.rationale: Thin Series B or extension round, used when growth slowed after the Series A and investors price the company on revenue multiples alone.
Central band; 2022 and later Series B median is $40M.
Hot company band; 2022 and later post money median is $600M.
Breakout upside where one lead investor competes hard for a category leader with fast revenue growth and strong net retention.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series B in under two years would require rapid scaling to many health systems with measured recovered revenue, which almost no vertical healthcare AI company does. Candid Health (W20) took four years from YC to its Series B, and Arintra needed more than three years to get a Series B, so the window is too short for this step except in a breakout.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series C within the window is close to impossible for a company that started with three people. Candid Health reached its later rounds only after about five years and large payer integrations. Any such outcome would need a category defining revenue ramp and a hospital system or payer channel partnership not visible today.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company stalls as one of many AI denial tools: payers and hospitals adopt platform offerings from large RCM vendors, or the team pivots to a broader RCM product. Past analogs Semantix (S17), Argovox (S22) and Remy (S23) are listed as inactive with no recorded funding, and CombineHealth has not shown a priced round after two years.

killers.evidence: CombineHealth (W23), Egress Health (W25) and Substrate era players target the same RCM spend, and large vendors such as Waystar and R1 already sell denial tools.
killers.mitigation: Pick one payer and one denial type with measured overturn rates before widening.

killers.risk: Long hospital sales cycles and integration work
killers.evidence: Hospital procurement and EHR or clearinghouse integrations take many months and a three person team has limited capacity to support them.
killers.mitigation: Start with independent billing companies and physician groups that buy faster.

killers.evidence: Premier puts the cost of appealing a denial near $57 per claim and many small claims are never worth reworking, while payers are adding their own AI.
killers.mitigation: Price on recovered revenue and focus on high dollar denials where appeals pay back.

technical_complexity.rationale: Drafting appeals with language models is easy to prototype; the hard parts are payer specific rules, clinical documentation retrieval from many EHRs and measured accuracy. A small team can ship a narrow version in three months but integrations take longer.

takeover_risk.rationale: Large revenue cycle vendors already have denial modules and distribution, and adding a language model appeals agent is a quarter or two of work for them, so the wedge is easy to absorb unless Aegis wins on recovery results.

evidence.claim: Initial denial rates near 12 percent for hospitals in 2024, with appeal cost about $57 per claim and large write-offs
Between 35 and 65 percent of denied claims are never reworked, showing unmet demand

roadmap.proof: Documented dollars recovered above software cost

actions: Publish case studies with overturn rates
Add integrations with the top 2 billing systems
roadmap.proof: $30K or more monthly revenue and 10 live customers

actions: Get SOC 2 and HIPAA audits done

pros.point: Clear dollar pain and measurable ROI
pros.evidence: Denials cost providers billions and the appeal cost is quantified at $57 per claim, so recovery can be sold on results.
Revenue cycle automation attracts funding and Candid Health and Arintra from YC reached later rounds.

brand.name: Aegis
weaknesses: Common name used by many security and insurance firms, so hard to own the search term
brand.rationale: Aegis means protection and suits a claims defense product, but the word is used by many companies, so it will not drive growth; short invented style names such as Candid Health (W20) show a name rarely decides the outcome.

narrative.headline: A real paid pain in a crowded AI revenue cycle category; a priced seed inside 19 months is slightly below even odds.
narrative.general_summary: Aegis automates health insurance denial appeals with AI agents for provider billing teams. The pain is large and measurable, but the category was already crowded by April 2025 and the team is three people with no stated customers. Inside a 19 month window the seed probability follows the Healthcare cohort timing, not a lift for the hot sector. A Series A inside the window is unlikely. The odds do not rank Aegis against other companies. If it raises, the most likely size is a $3M to $6M institutional seed, and the paths that matter most are proof of recovered dollars, a few paying billing teams and a clear edge over large revenue cycle vendors that can copy the idea within a few quarters.
